narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the rulers take counsel together' - deliberation, minds pooled into a single plan. Type (102) is cognition: this is a thinking act, planning and conferring, not a felt state nor a bare deed. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked, so the reading does not trace what drives the plotting - not fear, not ambition - it reports the deliberation without naming its spring. Seat (104) resolves to none: the counsel is not organ-located but the persons' concerted planning, held by the powerful as such, not the working of an inner faculty. Bearer (105) is the rulers - the kings of the earth, whose collective interior is read here. Operation (106), the core event, is that the kings and rulers conspire in concert against the LORD and his Anointed - organised rebellion, cognition turned into coordinated revolt. Target (107) is 'conspiracy': the deliberation aims at a plot, the joint scheme itself. Manner (108) is none - no mode marked, the conferring reported flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are all absent: no degree of the plotting is scored, nothing narrows it, and no downstream outcome is booked - the LORD's answering derision (v4) is not filed as this operation's effect. Coupling (112) is 'take-counsel': the reading is welded to the very act of counselling together, plural minds bound in one aim. Prohibition (113) is absent - not forbidden in this row, though the whole psalm indicts the revolt. Discovery (114) names it: the plot organises into a conspiracy of the powerful, deliberation turned to coordinated revolt. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a shared inner posture held within, even as it issues in outward alliance. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the rulers' collective mind pools into an organised conspiracy against the LORD and his Anointed - cognition welded to concerted counsel, an inward resolve of the powerful that turns thought into revolt. Read at full weight, this is the mind's gift of deliberation bent to rebellion.
narratives.story: The psalm opens on the world's rulers with their heads together. Kings and princes are pooling their minds and laying plans - but the plan is a plot, and the plot is against the Lord and the king he has anointed. This is the mind's power to think and confer, here bent to rebellion: many rulers reasoning as one, their scheming fused into a single conspiracy. The passage never tells us what is driving them, whether fear or ambition; it simply shows the shared deliberation and where it is aimed. It is a settled inner resolve that shows itself in their banding together. Nothing here spells out the verdict, but the picture is unmistakable - good sense, the gift of taking counsel, turned into organised revolt.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be wise, be warned' - wisdom issued as an imperative to rebel kings. Type (102) is cognition: an act of the understanding, being brought to sober sense. Source (103) is absent: the reading books no origin for the summons behind the verse - it reports the call, not who supplies the wisdom. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the wisdom urged is the persons' own reconsidering, not an inner organ switched on. Bearer (105) is the kings - the same rebellious rulers of v2, now addressed. Operation (106) is the turn: the kings are summoned to prudence, to be warned - the interior called back from revolt to sober sense. Target (107) is 'summons-to-prudence': what the operation aims at is the rousing of good sense in the rebel, wisdom offered as reconsideration. Manner (108) is none - the charge stands plainly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows the wisdom, and no outcome is booked - whether the kings heed is left open. Coupling (112) is 'be-wise': welded to the paired imperative to be warned. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the psalm calls the rebellious interior to reconsider; wisdom offered as the off-ramp from ruin. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition the will is charged to enter. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the psalm commands the rebel kings' interior to become wise and take warning - a cognition-turn, wisdom held out to the very minds that had pooled into conspiracy, the sober sense that would pull them back from destruction.
narratives.story: The same kings who were plotting against God and his anointed are now, at the end of the psalm, told plainly: be wise, be warned. Wisdom here is a command aimed straight at rebels - a call to come to their senses. The passage does not say where the wisdom is to come from; it simply holds it out as the way back from ruin. It is paired with a warning, and it is left open whether they will take it. In short, good sense is offered as an off-ramp to minds set on revolt - the chance to reconsider before it is too late.
narratives.variation_note: The same word for being wise recurs at Psa 94:8 (reading H7919:wise#2), and the difference is a finding. Here at Psa 2:10 the wisdom is read as a cognition summoned as an imperative to rebel kings - the sober sense that would turn them from an organised revolt already under way, an off-ramp from ruin. At Psa 94:8 it is read as a disposition the fools are urged toward - the discernment lacked by those who imagine God does not see. Both are calls to the senseless to become wise, but this reading foregrounds the sharp turn demanded of the powerful mid-rebellion, while the other foregrounds a settled discernment the dull are pressed to acquire.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'counsel in the soul, sorrow in the heart' - the mind turning over its own case. Type (102) is cognition: an inner deliberating, thinking rather than feeling, though it is shadowed by sorrow. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind the churn - the reading reports the deliberation without tracing what first set it going, though the psalm's unanswered 'how long' hangs over it. Seat (104) is none: for all that soul and heart are named, the operation is not treated as organ-located; soul and heart read as the whole inner person consulting itself, not a faculty switched on. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - his own interior, read from within. Operation (106) is the core event: the self carries a wearying inner deliberation, taking counsel in its soul with sorrow in its heart all day - the churn of unrelieved anxiety. Target (107) is 'inner-churn': the deliberation has no outward object but turns back on itself, self-consultation that finds no rest. Manner (108) is none - no mode marked. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: the 'all the day' of the verse is carried in the operation itself, not scored as a separate degree; nothing narrows it and no outcome is booked. Coupling (112) is 'counsel-and-sorrow': the deliberation is welded to grief - thinking and sorrowing move together, the counsel bitter because sorrow renews with it. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the exhausting round of self-consultation that finds no rest, sorrow renewed daily. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - wholly inward, a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist's mind turns over its own trouble all day long, taking counsel with itself and finding no answer, the deliberation welded to a sorrow that renews with every round - an inner churn that is cognition without relief, wisdom's faculty of counsel turned into a wearying self-consultation.
narratives.story: Here counsel is not a plan made with others but the mind wearing itself out on its own trouble. The psalmist takes counsel in his soul, turning his case over and over inside himself, all day long, with sorrow sitting in his heart the whole time. The thinking has no outward aim; it just circles back on itself and finds no answer. And it is bound tightly to grief - every round of self-consultation renews the sorrow. The passage does not say what first set this churning going, only that it will not stop and will not rest. It is the mind's good power to deliberate, here turned into an exhausting inner round that only deepens the ache.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the fool says no God' - nabal, the moral fool. Type (102) is cognition: this is an interior verdict, a thing said in the heart, not merely a deed. Source (103) is absent: no driver is booked behind the denial - the reading gives the verdict without naming what produced it. Seat (104) is none: the operation is not organ-located; though it is said 'in his heart', heart here reads as the whole inner person, not a faculty-organ. Bearer (105) is the fool - his interior read from within. Operation (106) is the core event: the fool says in his heart there is no God - a moral-practical denial that issues in corrupt deeds. Target (107) is 'practical-atheism': not a philosophy but a lived premise, God ruled out in practice. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows the denial, and the abominable deeds are read as what the denial issues in rather than filed as a separate booked effect. Coupling (112) is 'no-God-in-heart': the verdict is welded to its inward seat, a premise carried in the heart. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the operation is an interior verdict (not a philosophy) that clears the way for abominable deeds - denial as licence. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no booked source and no organ-seat, the fool's interior pronounces there is no God - a practical, not intellectual, denial welded to the heart that carries it, and this inward verdict licenses the corruption and abominable deeds that follow. This is folly at its root: not ignorance of facts but a heart that has cleared God out of its reckoning.
narratives.story: The fool of this psalm is not a stupid man but a morally reckless one, and his folly is a sentence he passes inside himself: there is no God. It is not a worked-out argument; it is a lived assumption, God quietly ruled out of the picture. The passage does not say what led him there, only that once the verdict is in, the way is clear for corrupt and abominable deeds - the denial acts as a licence. It is carried in the heart, and from that inner premise everything foul flows. This is folly at its deepest: not a lack of information but a heart that has cleared God out of its accounts.
narratives.variation_note: The same figure recurs at Psa 53:1 (reading H5036:fool#2), in what is nearly a twin psalm, and the coding difference is a finding. Here at Psa 14:1 the fool is read as a cognition - an interior verdict, the denial itself, with no seat named (the heart standing for the whole person). At Psa 53:1 the same words are read as a status, with an explicit seat (the heart), a manner (inwardly), and the denial coupled as what issues in corruption and abominable deeds. Both name practical atheism, the same premise from which corruption flows; but this reading foregrounds the act of the denial, while the other foregrounds the fool's settled condition and its lodging in the heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the simple made wise' - the untrained interior brought to understanding. Type (102) is cognition: a maturing of the understanding, not a feeling or a bare act. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, yet the verse names the agent within the operation: it is the sure testimony of the LORD that makes wise - so the reading carries the maker inside the event rather than tracing it as a separate source. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the simple person is made wise as a whole, not by a faculty switched on. Bearer (105) is the simple - the naive, untrained interior that lacks understanding. Operation (106) is the core event: the sure testimony of the LORD makes the simple wise - an interior maturing from naivety to wisdom. Target (107) is 'maturing': what the operation aims at is the growth itself, understanding raised where there was none. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree of the wisdom is scored, nothing narrows it, and no separate outcome is booked. Coupling (112) is 'simple-made-wise': the reading is welded to that very transformation, the pairing of the naive and the wise it becomes. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the opening of an untrained interior; the word grows understanding where there was none. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the change is a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no separately booked source but with the LORD's sure testimony named as the maker within the event, the simple, untrained interior is grown into wisdom - a cognition-maturing that raises understanding where there was none, held wholly within as a new inner condition. Wisdom here is not achieved but received: the word opens a mind that had none.
narratives.story: This psalm praises God's word for what it does inside a person, and one of its works is to make the simple wise. The 'simple' here is the untrained, naive mind that has no understanding of its own. God's sure testimony grows that mind up - it matures from naivety into real wisdom. The change is the whole point: understanding raised where there was none before. And notice the direction - the person does not achieve this wisdom by effort; it is given, worked in from outside by the word, and it becomes a settled new condition of the inner life. Wisdom here is received, not earned: the word opens a mind that had nothing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'I will teach you the fear of the LORD' - instruction offered outward. Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, the interior choosing to hand on what it holds. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind the impulse to teach - the reading reports the resolve, not what first kindled it. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the teaching is the person's willed act, not a faculty operating. Bearer (105) is the teacher - the psalmist turned instructor. Operation (106) is the core event: the self calls children to listen and be taught the fear of the LORD - passing on reverence. Target (107) is 'teaching-reverence': the aim is to plant fear of the LORD in another interior. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome (whether the children learn) is booked. Coupling (112) is 'teach-the-fear': welded to its very content, the fear of the LORD it means to transmit. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the operation turns instructor - the interior wants to hand its reverence to others. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the teaching impulse is a condition of the inner life, though it reaches outward. The full process: from no named source and no seat, the psalmist's will turns outward and summons children to be taught the fear of the LORD - a volition welded to that reverence, the inner life seeking to reproduce itself in another, held within as a settled disposition to instruct. Wisdom here is not kept but given away: the reverent interior wants company in its fear.
narratives.story: After a whole psalm of tasting how good the Lord is, the psalmist turns teacher: come, children, listen, and I will teach you the fear of the Lord. This is an act of the will - a person deciding to hand on what he himself holds. What he wants to pass along is reverence, the fear of the Lord, planted now in younger hearts. The passage does not say what first moved him to teach, and it does not tell us whether the children take it in; it simply shows the settled desire to instruct. It is a settled inner desire that reaches outward. Wisdom here is not hoarded but given away - a reverent heart wanting others to share its awe of God.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb for teaching recurs at Psa 143:10 (reading H3925:teach#2), and the direction reverses - a finding. Here at Psa 34:11 the operation is outward: the psalmist as teacher, willing to hand the fear of the LORD to children, reverence reproduced in others. At Psa 143:10 the same willing is inward and receptive: the psalmist asks God to teach him to do his will. Both are acts of the will about instruction, but this reading foregrounds the giving of wisdom to others, while the other foregrounds the hunger to be taught oneself.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'he has ceased to act wisely' - a stopping, a giving-up. Type (102) is volition: this is a chosen abdication, an act of the will, not a mere lapse. Source (103) is absent: no driver is booked behind the ceasing - though the psalm names transgression speaking in his heart and no fear of God before his eyes (vv1-2), the reading files the abdication itself without tracing its spring. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; it is the person's willed abandonment, not a faculty failing. Bearer (105) is the wicked - the man whose interior is opened in vv1-4. Operation (106) is the core event: the words of his mouth are trouble and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely and do good - a deliberate giving-up of wisdom. Target (107) is 'abandonment-of-good': what the act aims at is the surrender itself, wisdom and good let go. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome is booked. Coupling (112) is 'ceased-wise': welded to the wisdom it drops, defined by what it abandons. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): a chosen abdication - the interior has stopped even trying to be wise or good. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a settled inner condition. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the wicked man's will lets go of wisdom and good together - not a slip but a deliberate ceasing, welded to the very wisdom it abandons, held within as a settled condition of the inner life. This is folly as surrender: not the mind that never had wisdom but the will that has quit it.
narratives.story: This psalm looks inside a wicked man and finds, at the centre, a decision to stop. He has ceased to act wisely and to do good - and the word is a giving-up, not a stumble. His mouth runs to trouble and deceit, and behind the speech is a will that has quit even trying to be wise or good. The passage does not spell out what drove him there, though it has already noted that he has no fear of God before his eyes; it simply records the abandonment. It is a settled state now, defined by exactly what he has let go. This is folly of a particular kind - not a mind that never knew better, but a will that has walked away from what it knew.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'my wounds fester through my folly' - injury that rots. Type (102) is state: not an act nor a felt spike but a condition the body carries, wounds in their festering. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, yet the verse names the cause within the operation: the festering is 'because of my foolishness' - so folly is carried inside the event as its ground rather than traced as a separate source. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the wounds are the whole self's, not lodged in a named inner organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - his own body and self. Operation (106) is the core event: the self's wounds stink and fester because of its foolishness - self-inflicted rot from folly. Target (107) is 'festering-folly': the condition centres on folly's fruit, the rot itself. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no further outcome is booked - the festering is the state, not a step to something else. Coupling (112) is 'wounds-fester': welded to the process of festering, the rot inseparable from the wound. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): distinct from the sin-sickness of the psalm, this names the wounds as the fruit of the self's own folly, corrupting from within. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - held within, though it surfaces in the body. The full process: from folly named as the ground within the event and no separate seat, the psalmist's wounds stink and fester - a self-inflicted rot that folly has produced, a bodily condition traced back to his own foolishness, corrupting from within. Here folly is not merely a mistake but a poison: it rots the one who carries it.
narratives.story: In the middle of a psalm heavy with sickness and sin, one line traces the rot to its root: my wounds stink and fester because of my foolishness. This is a condition, not an action - festering wounds the man carries. And the passage is blunt about the cause: it is his own folly that has done this. The wounds are self-inflicted, the fruit of foolishness working like a poison in the body. Nothing in the verse points outward to blame; the corruption comes from within, from the man's own folly turning back on him. Here folly is shown not as a harmless slip but as something that literally festers - it rots the person who lives by it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wisdom' (chokmah) - skilled insight held and offered. Type (102) is status: a possessed condition of the inner being, the teacher's inner store, not a single act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked for the wisdom - it is presented as already possessed, not traced to its acquiring. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the wisdom is held by the whole person, not lodged in a named inner organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - the teacher who addresses all peoples, high and low. Operation (106) is 'speak': the store of wisdom overflows into speech, the interior brought to utterance. Target (107) is none: no object the wisdom is aimed at is booked - the reading reports the wisdom overflowing into speech, not pointed at a named end (the 'all peoples' are the audience, not filed as target). Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome is booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the heart's understanding' (span-resolved): the wisdom of the mouth is welded to the meditation of the heart that is understanding - speech and inner reflection move together, the spoken wisdom drawn from an understanding heart. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the teacher's inner store of wisdom overflowing into speech, chokmah the skilled insight the psalmist offers all peoples, high and low, rich and poor. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - the wisdom is a condition of the inner life that surfaces in speech. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the psalmist holds wisdom as a settled inner store and speaks it out to all peoples, its utterance welded to an understanding heart - a possessed condition of the inner being that overflows into teaching, wisdom not aimed at a single target but poured out for high and low alike.
narratives.story: The psalmist calls the whole world to listen - rich and poor, high and low - and tells them what he is about to give: my mouth shall speak wisdom. Here wisdom is something he already has, a settled store inside him, and now it overflows into speech. It is paired with the quiet work of his heart: the understanding he has meditated on is what his mouth pours out, so inner reflection and spoken wisdom move together. He does not aim it at any one target; he simply offers it to everyone. This is wisdom as a possession of the inner life that cannot stay silent - insight held within, brimming over into teaching for all.
narratives.variation_note: This is the first of four readings of wisdom (chokmah) in the family, and the differences among them are findings. Here at Psa 49:3 wisdom is a status - a teacher's possessed inner store that overflows into speech for all peoples, coupled to the understanding heart. At Psa 51:6 it is wisdom God implants in the secret heart (a status seated in the heart, received not held). At Psa 90:12 it is a disposition gained by numbering our days in the face of death. At Psa 111:10 it is a disposition that flows from the fear of the LORD. This reading foregrounds wisdom already owned and given away in teaching, where the others foreground wisdom received - implanted, learned from mortality, or rooted in reverence.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'stupid / brutish' (baar) - beast-like senselessness. Type (102) is status: a condition of the person, not an act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked for the stupidity. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the brutishness belongs to the whole person, not a faculty. Bearer (105) is the brutish - the senseless man set alongside the fool. Operation (106) is none: the reading books no act for the stupid one - and the silence is telling, for in this passage the brutish does nothing but perish; his stupidity is not shown working but simply ending in death. Target (107) is none: no object, consistent with an operation that is none - the condition has no aim, only an end. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome is booked beyond the perishing carried in the passage. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the fool' (span-resolved): the brutish is welded to the fool - the two named together, sharing one fate. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the brutish/animal-like senseless, baar the beast-like stupidity, echoing 'like the beasts that perish', perishing and leaving wealth behind. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no source, no act, no target, and no manner - only a bare status welded to the fool - the brutish man is read as pure senseless condition that does nothing and simply perishes with the fool, leaving his wealth to others. The heavy silence across operation and target is the point: this stupidity is not a doing but a being, a beast-like dullness whose only movement is toward the grave, levelled by death exactly as the fool is.
narratives.story: In this meditation on death and money, the stupid man appears beside the fool, and the striking thing is how little he does. He does not act, he does not aim at anything - the passage gives him no deed at all. He is simply brutish, beast-like and senseless, and the one thing that happens to him is that he perishes, like the animals, leaving his wealth behind for others. His stupidity is not a busy scheming; it is a condition, a dullness of being. And he is bound to the fool, the two of them named together and dying together. The whole point of the silence around him is that his senselessness is not something he does but something he is - and it ends, like the beasts, in the grave.
narratives.variation_note: The same word (baar) recurs at Psa 92:6 (reading H1198:stupid#2), and the difference is a finding. Here at Psa 49:10 the stupid man is read as a bare status with no operation and no target - he does nothing; his senselessness is simply a condition that ends in death alongside the fool. At Psa 92:6 the same stupidity is given an operation ('be brutish/senseless') and a target (unable to know God's works) - the dullness there is shown actively failing to grasp God's deep purposes. This reading foregrounds stupidity as a mortal condition levelled by death; the other foregrounds it as a live incapacity before God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wise' (chakam) - the genuinely wise person. Type (102) is status: a settled condition, not an act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked for the wisdom. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; wisdom held by the whole person. Bearer (105) is the wise (who also die) - the sage read here precisely under the shadow of mortality. Operation (106) is 'die' (inferred): the one act booked to the wise here is not an exercise of wisdom but dying - the arresting move of the passage, wisdom's bearer shown doing the one thing wisdom cannot avert. Target (107) is none: death has no object; the wise simply die. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome beyond the leaving of wealth is booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the fool and stupid' (span-resolved): the wise is welded to the fool and the brutish - three named in one breath, sharing one grave. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): death levels even wisdom; chakam here the wise who, no less than the fool, must die and leave their wealth - mortality the common lot. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the wise man - a settled condition of real insight - is shown doing the one thing his wisdom cannot prevent: he dies, welded in death to the fool and the brutish, leaving his wealth to others. The finding is the levelling: wisdom is genuine, but the passage reads it under mortality, where the sage and the senseless meet the same end. Here wisdom's limit, not its power, is in view.
narratives.story: This psalm on death and riches makes a hard observation: even the wise die. The wise person here is genuinely wise - real insight, a settled quality of mind - but the one thing the passage shows him doing is dying. His wisdom, for all its worth, cannot buy him out of the grave. And he is named in the same breath as the fool and the brutish man: the three of them go down together and leave their wealth to others. Death does not care that one of them was wise. The point is not that wisdom is worthless but that it has a limit - at the edge of the grave, the sage and the senseless are levelled, and the wise man's insight cannot save him from the common end.
narratives.variation_note: The same word (chakam) recurs at Psa 107:43 (reading H2450:wise#2), and the contrast is a finding. Here at Psa 49:10 the wise man is read under mortality: the one act booked to him is to die, welded to the fool and the brutish, his wisdom shown at its limit. At Psa 107:43 the wise man is read at the height of his powers: 'whoever is wise, let him attend to these things' - wisdom actively discerning the steadfast love of the LORD in his dealings. This reading foregrounds wisdom levelled by death; the other foregrounds wisdom rightly reading God's ways.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fool' (kesil) - the thick-headed, dull fool. Type (102) is status: a settled condition. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fool - the dullard read here under mortality. Operation (106) is 'perish' (inferred): the one act booked to the fool is not a folly performed but perishing - the passage catches him at his end, not his antics. Target (107) is none: perishing has no object. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome beyond leaving wealth is booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the wise and the stupid' (span-resolved): the fool is welded to the wise and the brutish - the three named together, one fate. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the dullard's death alongside the wise; kesil the thick-headed fool who, with the wise, leaves his wealth to others. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no source and no seat, the dull fool is shown doing the same last thing the wise man does - he perishes, welded to the wise and the brutish, leaving his wealth behind. The finding is that death does not sort by wisdom: the fool's end is identical to the sage's. Here folly is read not in its foolish acts but at the grave, where it meets exactly the fate of wisdom.
narratives.story: In this psalm about death and wealth, the thick-headed fool appears - and, strikingly, the passage does not show him doing anything foolish. It shows him dying. Along with the wise man and the brutish man, he perishes and leaves his wealth to others. Death treats all three alike; it does not sort them by how wise or foolish they were. The fool is caught here not in his blunders but at his end, and his end is exactly the same as the sage's. It is a sobering flattening: at the grave, wisdom and folly come out level, and the fool goes down with everyone else.
narratives.variation_note: This is the first of three readings of the fool (kesil) in the family. Here at Psa 49:10 the fool is read under mortality - the one thing booked to him is to perish, alongside the wise and the brutish, wealth left behind. At Psa 92:6 he is read as unable to understand God's justice in history (an active incapacity). At Psa 94:8 he is the one who thinks God does not see, rebuked and urged toward wisdom. This reading foregrounds the fool at the grave, levelled with the wise; the others foreground his live blindness to God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'foolish confidence / folly' (kesel) - misplaced self-assurance. Type (102) is status: a settled condition, the way a person is. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked for the confidence. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the confidence belongs to the whole person. Bearer (105) is those of foolish confidence - the rich who trust in their wealth. Operation (106) is none: no act is booked - and the silence fits, for this folly is read as a way one is, a stance of self-trust, not a deed performed. Target (107) is none: no object, consistent with a status that simply is. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and no outcome is booked (the grave-end is the psalm's frame, not filed here as this operation's effect). Coupling (112) is 'whose boasts people approve' (span-resolved): the foolish confidence is welded to the applause it draws - others endorse the boast, so the folly is socially reinforced, admired even as it ends in the grave. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the self-assured folly that trusts in wealth; kesel the misplaced confidence of the rich, a way that ends in the grave yet is admired by those who follow. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no source, no act, and no target - only a bare status - the folly is read as a settled self-confidence of the wealthy, welded to the approval of onlookers who applaud the boast even though the path ends in death. The finding is folly's social respectability: this is not a hidden vice but an admired stance, misplaced trust in riches that the crowd endorses right up to the grave.
narratives.story: This psalm names a particular folly: the smug self-confidence of the rich, who trust in their money. It is not shown doing anything - it is simply a way of being, a settled stance of trusting in wealth. What makes it chilling is the company it keeps: people approve of the boast. The confident rich are admired, their swagger applauded by those who come after them - and yet the whole path ends in the grave. So this folly is not a shameful secret; it is respectable, even envied. The passage lets us see it plainly: a misplaced trust that the crowd cheers on, right up to the moment it walks into death.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'discipline / instruction' (musar) - corrective training. Type (102) is status: it names a thing, discipline as such, the correction one may love or spurn. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is discipline itself, marked here as hated by the wicked - a striking framing: the char-item is not a movement of the wicked's interior but the correction that his interior rejects. Operation (106) is none: no act is booked to discipline - it does not here do anything; it is done-to, the object of a reaction. Target (107) is none: consistent with an operation that is none. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'the object of the wicked's hatred' (span-resolved): discipline is welded to the wicked's hatred of it - defined here by the rejection it meets, cast behind him with God's words. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the correction the wicked refuses; musar = instruction/chastening, the very thing the wise love and the wicked spurn, casting God's words behind them. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - discipline as a condition/good of the inner life. The full process: discipline is read not as an act the interior performs but as a good the interior meets and either receives or rejects; here it is booked entirely through the wicked's hatred - no source, no operation, no target of its own, only its status as the hated correction cast behind him. The finding is by contrast: the same instruction the wise love, the wicked despises, and his contempt for correction marks his folly. Discipline is shown by its refusal.
narratives.story: Here the study looks at discipline - the kind of correction and training that shapes a person - by watching what the wicked do with it: they hate it. Discipline itself does nothing in this verse; it is on the receiving end. God's words come as instruction, and the wicked man throws them behind his back. The passage defines the correction almost entirely by the reaction it meets - the very thing a wise person welcomes, this man despises. And that contempt is the giveaway. To hate correction, to want no training and no rebuke, is itself the mark of folly. Discipline is shown to us here not by someone embracing it but by someone flinging it away.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wisdom' (chokmah) - here the wisdom taught in the secret heart. Type (102) is status: a condition of the inner being, but a received one. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though the operation names God as the one who teaches it. Seat (104) carries a value: 'in the secret heart' - unlike most readings in the family, this wisdom is organ-located, lodged in the hidden inner self. Bearer (105) is the penitent - David laid open before God. Operation (106) is none: no act is booked to the wisdom itself - it is not shown working but being implanted, a thing received rather than a thing done. Target (107) is none: consistent with a received status. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'the object of God's inner teaching' (span-resolved): the wisdom is welded to God's teaching in the secret heart - it exists here only as what God implants, paired with the truth God delights in in the inward being. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wisdom God implants in the hidden self; chokmah here not the sage's craft but the reordering of the inner life toward truth - the fruit of God's teaching in the depths. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:heart - lodged in the heart, the hidden inner self. The full process: seated in the secret heart and coupled as the object of God's inner teaching, this wisdom is a received condition of the penitent's interior - not a craft he exercises but a reordering God works in his depths, an implanted wisdom the sinner asks for where he most desires truth. The finding is location and passivity together: wisdom here sits in the hidden heart and is received, not performed - the remaking of the inner life from within.
narratives.story: Praying after his great sin, David does not ask for cleverness or skill; he says that God teaches wisdom in the secret heart. This wisdom is different from a sage's talent - it is something God works deep in the hidden self, in the innermost place where God also delights in truth. And notice, David does not do anything with it here; he receives it. It is implanted, not exercised - a quiet reordering of his inner life toward what is true, worked by God in his depths. Unlike wisdom that a person holds and shows off, this one is lodged in the secret heart and given by God. It is the remaking of a man from the inside, exactly where he most needs to be honest.
narratives.variation_note: This is the second of four wisdom (chokmah) readings, and it stands apart. Unlike Psa 49:3, where wisdom is a teacher's possessed store spoken out, here at Psa 51:6 wisdom is received - seated in the secret heart (a rare seat value in the family) and coupled as the object of God's inner teaching, not performed but implanted. It differs from Psa 90:12 (wisdom gained by numbering our days) and Psa 111:10 (wisdom rooted in the fear of the LORD) in its location and passivity: this is wisdom lodged in the hidden heart and worked by God in the depths, the reordering of the inner life toward truth rather than an insight the person acquires or exercises.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'make known / teach' (yada, hiphil) - here 'you teach me wisdom'. Type (102) is action: a doing, teaching as an act, though the penitent is on its receiving end. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though God is the teacher within the operation. Seat (104) carries a value: 'in the secret heart' - the teaching reaches the hidden inner self, organ-located in the depths. Bearer (105) is the penitent (taught) - David, the one instructed. Operation (106) is 'be taught / made to know': the event is the receiving of instruction, the hidden self opened to God's teaching. Target (107) is 'wisdom' (span-resolved): what is taught is wisdom itself, knowledge worked into the depths. Manner (108) carries a value: 'in the secret heart' - the how is that this teaching happens inwardly, in the hidden place, not by external drill. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no separate outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with truth in the inward being' (span-resolved): the teaching is welded to God's delight in truth in the inward being - instruction and truth-in-the-depths belong together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the inner instruction the penitent receives; the hidden self opened to God's teaching, wisdom implanted where he desires truth - knowledge not of facts but of the reordered inner life. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:heart - the teaching lands in the heart, the hidden inner self. The full process: seated and conducted in the secret heart, welded to the truth God delights in in the inward being, this teaching is God making wisdom known in the penitent's depths - an action received rather than performed, whose target is wisdom and whose whole manner is inwardness. The finding is that real instruction here is not information delivered to the surface but wisdom worked into the hidden self, the reordering of the inner life from within.
narratives.story: In the same prayer, David speaks of God teaching him - and the teaching goes to a hidden place. God, he says, makes wisdom known to him in the secret heart. This is not a lesson learned by the ears; it is instruction that reaches the innermost self, right where God delights in honesty. David is on the receiving end: he is being taught, made to know, and what he is being taught is wisdom itself. The whole thing happens inwardly - in the depths, not on the surface, and it is bound up with God's love of truth in the inner being. So the teaching here is not facts handed over but a reordering of a man's inner life, wisdom pressed into the hidden heart where it can actually change him.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb (yada, teach) recurs at Psa 78:5 (reading H3045:teach#2), and the difference is a finding. Here at Psa 51:6 the teaching is inward and received: God teaches the penitent wisdom in the secret heart, seated and conducted in the depths, welded to truth in the inward being - the reordering of one man's hidden self. At Psa 78:5 the teaching is outward and transmissive: the fathers are commanded to teach the law to their children, generation to generation, located in the community (external:person). This reading foregrounds God's private instruction of the individual heart; the other foregrounds the public handing-on of God's testimony to the young.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fool' (nabal) - the moral fool who says there is no God. Type (102) is status: a settled condition of the person, not merely a passing thought. Source (103) is absent: no driver is booked behind the denial. Seat (104) carries a value: 'the heart' (span-resolved) - here, unlike the twin at Psa 14:1, the denial is explicitly organ-located in the heart, the seat of the fool's premise. Bearer (105) is the fool (nabal) - his interior read from within. Operation (106) is 'say (in his heart)' (inferred): the event is the inward pronouncing, 'there is no God.' Target (107) is 'there is no God' (inferred): what he says to himself, the content of the denial. Manner (108) carries a value: 'inwardly, in the heart' (span-resolved) - the how is that this is said not aloud as argument but privately, as a lived premise. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and the corruption is read through coupling rather than booked as effect. Coupling (112) is 'issues in corruption and abominable deeds' (span-resolved): the denial is welded to the corruption and abominable deeds that flow from it - the premise and its rotten fruit inseparable. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): practical atheism, not intellectual denial; nabal the one who lives as if God does not see - the inward premise from which corruption and abominable deeds flow; twin of Psa 14 (here 'Elohim' for YHWH). Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: seated in the heart and said inwardly, with no booked source, the fool pronounces 'there is no God' - a practical, not philosophical, denial that is welded to the corruption and abominable deeds it produces. The finding, against its twin, is the explicit lodging in the heart and the named issue in corruption: this folly is a heart-premise with a moral harvest, God ruled out where deeds are decided.
narratives.story: This psalm, almost a twin of Psalm 14, opens with the same reckless folly: the fool says in his heart, there is no God. It is not a philosophy he argues; it is a verdict he passes privately, deep in the heart, living as if God cannot see. Here the passage is pointed about where it happens - in the heart - and about what comes of it: from that inward denial flow corruption and abominable deeds. The premise and its rotten fruit cannot be separated; once God is ruled out where a man's decisions are made, the deeds turn foul. This is folly at its most practical and most dangerous: not a mistake about facts, but a heart that has quietly decided God does not matter, and acts accordingly.
narratives.variation_note: This reading twins with Psa 14:1 (reading H5036:fool#1), and the coding difference is the finding. There the fool's denial is typed as a cognition with no seat named (the heart standing for the whole person). Here at Psa 53:1 the same words are typed as a status and given an explicit seat (the heart), an explicit manner (inwardly, in the heart), and a coupling that names the issue in corruption and abominable deeds. Both are practical atheism, the same heart-premise; but this reading foregrounds the settled condition, its lodging in the heart, and its moral harvest, where the twin foregrounds the bare act of denial.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'intimate counsel / close fellowship' (sod) - shared confidence, sweet counsel taken together. Type (102) is status: a relationship-condition, the closeness two shared, not a single act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked for the intimacy. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the fellowship belongs to the persons, not an inner organ. Bearer (105) is the psalmist and the friend - two interiors joined, now sundered. Operation (106) is 'share intimate counsel' (inferred): the event is the mutual confiding, minds and hearts opened to each other. Target (107) is none: no object beyond the sharing itself - the counsel is not aimed at a scheme but is the closeness. Manner (108) carries a value: 'sweet, walking to God's house in the throng' (span-resolved) - the how is warmth and shared worship, the intimacy deepened by going up to God's house together. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'the closeness of the familiar friend' (span-resolved): the counsel is welded to the bond of the familiar friend - the intimacy and the friendship one and the same. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the cherished intimacy now betrayed; sod the trusting fellowship, deepened by worshipping together - the very sweetness of it measures the bitterness of the breach. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:person - unusually, the counsel is located not within the self but in the bond with another; its reference-point is the friend. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, two interiors shared sweet, intimate counsel, welded to the closeness of the familiar friend and deepened by worship together in God's house - a relationship-condition located outside the self, in the other. The finding is set by betrayal: this counsel is here remembered precisely because it was broken; its sweetness, and its lodging in the friend rather than the self, measure the depth of the wound.
narratives.story: Amid the pain of betrayal, the psalmist remembers something tender: we used to take sweet counsel together. This kind of counsel is not plotting or planning - it is closeness, two friends opening their hearts to each other in trust. The passage makes it warmer still: their intimacy was deepened by going up to God's house together, worshipping side by side in the crowd. The whole thing lived in the friendship - its home was the other person, the familiar friend. And that is exactly why it hurts so much now. The sweetness of the shared confidence is being measured against the bitterness of its breaking. He recalls the intimacy not to celebrate it but to show how deep the wound goes when a trusted friend turns against you.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'folly / foolishness' (ivveleth) - here the psalmist's own, confessed. Type (102) is status: a condition of the person owned before God. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the folly is the whole self's. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - who confesses it as his own even while protesting innocence of his enemies' charges. Operation (106) is 'known (by God)' (span-resolved): the one act booked is not the folly working but God's knowing of it - 'you know my folly' - the movement is God's seeing, the folly laid open. Target (107) is none: the folly aims at nothing; it is exposed, not exercised. Manner (108) carries a value: 'not hidden from God' (inferred) - the how is total disclosure, nothing concealed from the God who knows all. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the wrongs he has done' (span-resolved): the folly is welded to his actual wrongs - not a vague failing but bound to real deeds, both known to God. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): honest confession of real failings even while protesting innocence of the charges; ivveleth the psalmist's own foolishness, laid open before the God who knows all - no self-righteousness in his plea, only truth. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, the psalmist's own folly is read not as an act he performs but as a thing God knows and nothing hides from - welded to his real wrongs, owned before the God who sees all. The finding is the honesty: even while he protests he is wronged by his enemies, he does not claim to be faultless; he lays his folly open, refusing self-righteousness. Here folly is met not by denial but by confession.
narratives.story: Surrounded by people who hate him without cause, the psalmist could easily protest that he is perfectly innocent. Instead he says something honest: O God, you know my folly; my wrongs are not hidden from you. He owns his own foolishness. He does not parade it or explain it, and he does not do anything with it - he simply lays it open before the God who sees everything. It is tied to real wrongs he has actually done, not a vague admission. What is striking is the refusal to be self-righteous: he can insist he is wronged by his enemies and still confess that he himself is not faultless. Here a person meets his own folly not by hiding it but by bringing it, fully known, into the light of God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'brutish / stupid' (baar) - beast-like senselessness, here confessed by the psalmist. Type (102) is status: a condition he owns, not a deed. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though the psalm names its trigger - his soul embittered, pricked in heart by envy of the wicked (vv3, 21). Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the brutishness was the whole self's. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - looking back on what his resentment reduced him to. Operation (106) is 'be brutish' (inferred): the event is his being senseless, dull as an animal. Target (107) is 'toward God (like a beast)' (inferred): the brutishness is oriented Godward - he was like a beast before God, blind in his relation to him. Manner (108) carries a value: 'like a beast toward God' (inferred) - the how is animal dullness, sub-rational, in God's presence. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with his ignorance' (span-resolved): the brutishness is welded to his ignorance - senselessness and not-knowing together, one blindness. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the humbling self-recognition; baar the beast-like stupidity the psalmist confesses his envy reduced him to - honest admission that his resentment was not clever but sub-human, blind before God. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from the embittered, envious heart of the psalm's crisis, with no separately booked source and no seat, the psalmist confesses he became brutish - beast-like and ignorant, senseless toward God, his stupidity welded to his ignorance. The finding is the self-recognition: read at full weight, this is the descent named from the inside - a good man admitting that his envy of the wicked did not make him shrewd but stupid, dumb as an animal in the presence of God.
narratives.story: Looking back on a spiritual crisis, the psalmist makes a humbling admission. When he had let envy of the prosperous wicked embitter him, he says, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you. He is not describing an enemy here - he is describing himself. His resentment, which no doubt felt sharp and justified at the time, is now seen for what it really was: not clever but stupid, dull and sub-human, blind in the presence of God. His senselessness and his ignorance were one and the same blindness. This is folly named honestly from the inside - a good man confessing that bitterness had turned him, for a while, into something as dumb as an animal before the God who was holding his hand the whole time.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'foolish' (nabal) - the moral fool, here a whole people who revile God's name. Type (102) is status: a condition of the enemy people. Source (103) carries a value - the only booked source in the family: 'whom God is asked to remember' (v18, span-resolved). The reading traces the foolish people's reviling back to God's remembering: it is set before God as the one who must take note of this folly. This unusual presence of a source marks the reading - the folly is not left unaccounted but placed under God's remembrance. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the folly belongs to the people as such. Bearer (105) is the foolish enemy people - their collective interior. Operation (106) is 'revile God's name' (span-resolved): the event is the blaspheming, scorn hurled at the name of God. Target (107) is 'God's name' (span-resolved): what the folly aims at is the name of God, the object of its contempt. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'the foolish who scoff all the day (v22)' (span-resolved): the reviling is welded to the continual scoffing of v22 - folly and its relentless mockery bound together. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the godless folly behind the blasphemy; nabal the moral fool (as Psa 14:1, 'no God') whose contempt of God's name is the mark of his folly - the enemy not merely cruel but spiritually senseless, whom God is asked to remember. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: sourced under God's remembrance and welded to relentless scoffing, the foolish people's interior turns to reviling the name of God - a folly whose whole movement is contempt aimed at that name. The finding is twofold: this is the family's one reading with a named source, the folly placed under God's remembering; and it identifies the enemy's cruelty as, at root, spiritual senselessness - the moral fool of Psalm 14 now writ large as a blaspheming people.
narratives.story: Praying against enemies who mock God, the psalmist puts his finger on what is really wrong with them: they are a foolish people, and their folly shows itself in reviling God's name. This is the same reckless, godless folly seen in the fool who says there is no God - here spread across a whole hostile people. Their scorn is aimed straight at the name of God, and they keep it up all day long, scoffing without letting up. What is distinctive here is that the psalmist hands the whole thing over to God's memory: remember this, he prays - let God take note of their folly. So the enemy is not just cruel; at bottom they are spiritually senseless, blaspheming what they cannot see, and their folly is laid before the God who will not forget it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'teach' (yada, hiphil) - to make known, here from one generation to the next. Type (102) is action: a doing, the deliberate handing-on of instruction. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind the fathers' teaching, though the verse says God commanded it. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; teaching is the fathers' act, not an inner organ. Bearer (105) is our fathers - the generation charged to instruct. Operation (106) is 'teach / make known': the event is the transmission of God's testimony and law to the young. Target (107) is 'the law to their children' (inferred): what is taught, and to whom - God's law, handed to the next generation. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and the intended outcome (that the next generation might know and hope in God, vv6-7) is carried by the passage rather than booked here as this operation's effect. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the appointed testimony' (inferred): the teaching is welded to the testimony God established in Jacob - instruction bound to the fixed deposit it transmits. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the charge to instruct the young in God's testimony. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:person - the teaching is located not in the self but in the bond between generations, aimed at the children. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the fathers' willed action carries God's law and testimony to their children - teaching welded to the appointed testimony, located in the passing-on between generations. The finding is the outward, communal shape of this instruction: not God reordering one hidden heart but a people commanded to hand its knowledge of God down the line, so that children yet unborn might in turn know and tell.
narratives.story: This psalm is about memory across generations. God set up his law and his testimony in Israel and commanded the fathers to teach them to their children - and that teaching is the thing in view here. It is a deliberate act of handing on: the older generation passing God's law to the younger, so that children not yet born will one day know it and tell it to their own children. The instruction is tied to the fixed deposit it carries - God's established testimony - and its home is the link between parents and children. Unlike a private lesson worked in one person's heart, this is a whole people's task of keeping the knowledge of God alive by passing it down the line, generation after generation.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb (yada, teach) appears at Psa 51:6 (reading H3045:teach#1), and the contrast is a finding. There the teaching is inward and received - God implanting wisdom in one penitent's secret heart. Here at Psa 78:5 it is outward and transmissive: the fathers commanded to teach God's law to their children, located in the community between generations (external:person), welded to the appointed testimony. This reading foregrounds the public, generational handing-on of God's word; the other foregrounds God's private reordering of an individual heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'counsels' (moetsah) - self-devised plans. Type (102) is faculty: read here as a capacity of the will/mind, the people's own planning power. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind their counsels. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the counsels belong to the people, not a named organ. Bearer (105) is my people - Israel, whose interior God describes. Operation (106) is 'follow their own counsel': the event is their choosing to walk by their self-made plans. Target (107) is 'instead of God' (inferred): the counsels aim away from God - the plans are pursued in place of his ways. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the stubborn heart' (inferred): the counsels are welded to the stubborn heart God gave them over to - self-planning and hardness of heart together, one apostasy. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the self-devised plans they preferred to God's ways, autonomy as apostasy. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the people's own faculty of counsel turns them away from God - they follow their self-made plans instead of his ways, the counsels welded to the stubborn heart they were given over to. The finding is that this folly is autonomy: God's judgment is precisely to let them have their own counsel, so the capacity for planning, cut loose from God, becomes the very instrument of their apostasy. Self-direction here is not freedom but the shape of the fall.
narratives.story: God speaks of his people's refusal, and the judgment fits the crime: because they would not listen to him, he gave them over to their own stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels. Their 'counsels' are the plans they cook up for themselves - their own ideas about how to live. Here that planning power is turned the wrong way: they pursue their schemes instead of God's ways, self-direction taking the place of obedience. It is bound up with a stubborn heart, the two working as one turning-away. The chilling thing is that God's punishment is simply to let them have exactly what they wanted - their own counsel. So the ability to plan and choose, cut off from God, becomes the very thing that carries them into apostasy. Going their own way is not freedom here; it is the fall itself.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'folly' (kislah) - senseless self-confidence, sin seen as folly. Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent the people might resume, not a single act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the people - God's own people, warned. Operation (106) is 'fall into folly': the event is a turning-back, relapsing into the senseless confidence they had left. Target (107) is 'away from God' (inferred): the folly aims away from God, a turn from him back to self-trust. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the turning-back' (inferred): the folly is welded to the act of turning back - relapse and folly one movement. Prohibition (113) is absent as a booked row, yet the verse itself frames the whole thing as a warning: 'let them not turn back to folly' - so the reading carries an implicit prohibition even though no row scores it. Discovery (114): the senseless self-confidence the people must not resume, sin as folly. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no booked source and no seat, the people are warned not to fall back into folly - a disposition of senseless self-confidence, welded to the act of turning back, aimed away from God. The finding is that sin is named here as folly and set as a danger of relapse: God speaks peace to his people, and the one thing they must not do is turn again to their old senselessness. The prohibition, though not booked in its own row, hangs over the whole reading - folly as the road back they are told not to take.
narratives.story: As God promises to speak peace to his people, one warning is attached: let them not turn back to folly. Here folly is sin seen as senselessness - the foolish self-confidence the people had lived by before. It is a settled leaning they could slip back into, a relapse. The danger is that, having been forgiven and restored, they would turn again away from God toward their old self-trust. The whole verse is really a caution: peace is offered, but do not go back to that foolishness. So sin gets named for what it is - not clever independence but folly - and it is pictured as a road they are told not to take again, the temptation to return to the very senselessness God has just brought them out of.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wisdom' (chokmah) - here the wisdom that comes of facing death. Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent gained, not a possessed store nor a single act. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though the operation names its means - numbering our days. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is we (mankind) - the mortal 'we' of Moses' prayer, whose days pass under God's wrath. Operation (106) is 'gain wisdom': the event is the acquiring of a wise heart. Target (107) is 'from numbering our days' (inferred): the wisdom is drawn from reckoning our mortality - counting our few days is the source-within-the-event. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired with the heart' (inferred): the wisdom is welded to the heart - 'a heart of wisdom' - it is the inner life itself made wise, not a skill added. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wisdom that flows from facing death, the fruit of numbering our days. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: from no separately booked source but with the numbering of days named as its means, mankind asks to gain a heart of wisdom - a disposition welded to the heart, grown by reckoning how few and fleeting the days are. The finding is the root: this wisdom is not craft or cleverness but the sober inner sense that comes only from facing mortality - the fruit of counting one's days before a God under whose wrath they pass. Wisdom here is what death teaches the heart.
narratives.story: In a prayer soaked in the shortness of life - our years soon gone, swept away like grass - Moses asks for a very particular kind of wisdom: teach us to number our days, that we may get a heart of wisdom. This wisdom is not skill or cleverness; it is the sober good sense that comes only from honestly facing death. It grows out of counting how few our days really are. And notice where it settles: in the heart - it is the inner life itself made wise, not a trick added on. So the passage traces wisdom to an unlikely root: mortality. When a person truly reckons with how brief life is, before a God whose judgment they live under, the heart is finally made wise. Here wisdom is what death, faced honestly, teaches.
narratives.variation_note: This third wisdom (chokmah) reading traces the source of wisdom rather than its exercise. Unlike Psa 49:3 (a teacher's possessed store spoken out) and Psa 51:6 (wisdom implanted by God in the secret heart), here at Psa 90:12 wisdom is a disposition gained by numbering our days - the fruit of facing death, welded to the heart. It shares with Psa 111:10 the pattern of wisdom-from-a-root, but the root differs: there it flows from the fear of the LORD, here from the honest reckoning of mortality. This reading foregrounds death as the teacher of wisdom.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'stupid' (baar) - beast-like senselessness. Type (102) is status: a condition of the person. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the stupid man - here shown in active incapacity. Operation (106) is 'be brutish / senseless': the event is his dullness in action, failing to take in what is before him. Target (107) is 'unable to know God's works' (inferred): the stupidity aims at - or rather falls short of - the knowledge of God's works; it is dullness precisely toward God's deep purposes. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry, respectively, an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with the fool's failure to understand' - so the brutishness is welded to the fool's parallel failure and lodged as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the stupidity is coupled to the fool and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the brutish insensibility that misses God's deep purposes, dullness of heart. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the stupid man is brutish and senseless, unable to know God's works, his dullness welded to the fool's matching failure to understand and held as an inner condition. The finding, against the mortal-status reading of Psa 49:10, is that here the stupidity is live and Godward: not a condition merely ending in death but an active incapacity - the beast-like mind that looks at God's great and deep works and cannot take them in.
narratives.story: This Sabbath psalm marvels at how great and deep God's works and thoughts are - and then names who cannot see it: the stupid man cannot know this. His stupidity is not passive here; it is a dullness at work, a beast-like insensibility that looks right at God's deeds in the world and simply cannot take them in. He stands next to the fool, the two of them failing in the same way, and the failure is lodged deep inside him. What he is blind to is exactly the thing the psalm is celebrating: that although the wicked flourish for a moment, they are doomed, and God reigns forever. The senseless mind misses all of it. Here stupidity is shown as a live incapacity before God - not just a fate, but a blindness at the very point where God's purposes are on display.
narratives.variation_note: The same word (baar) reads differently at Psa 49:10 (reading H1198:stupid#1), and the difference is a finding. There the stupid man has no operation and no target - a bare mortal status that simply perishes with the fool. Here at Psa 92:6 he is given an operation ('be brutish/senseless') and a target (unable to know God's works) - the dullness is active and Godward, missing God's deep purposes. This reading foregrounds stupidity as a live incapacity before God; the other foregrounds it as a condition levelled by death.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fool' (kesil) - the thick-headed fool. Type (102) is status: a condition of the person. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fool - here shown in active incapacity. Operation (106) is 'be a fool': the event is his foolishness at work, failing to grasp. Target (107) is 'unable to understand God's ways' (inferred): the folly falls short precisely of understanding God's justice in history. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with the stupid man's ignorance' - so the fool's failure is welded to the stupid man's matching ignorance and lodged as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the folly is coupled to the stupid man and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the senseless one blind to God's justice in history. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the fool is a fool in action - unable to understand God's ways, his failure welded to the stupid man's ignorance and held within. The finding, against the mortal reading of Psa 49:10, is that here the fool's folly is a live blindness to God: he cannot grasp that the wicked's flourishing is temporary and their doom certain. Paired with the stupid man, he is the mind that looks at history and misses God's justice running through it.
narratives.story: Right beside the stupid man in this psalm stands the fool, and he shares the same failure: the fool cannot understand this. What he cannot understand is the psalm's central truth - that though the wicked shoot up like grass and seem to flourish, they are headed for destruction, while God stays on high forever. The fool looks at the same world and cannot see God's justice working through it. His folly here is not just a fate waiting for him; it is a live blindness, a thick-headedness at work. He and the stupid man fail together, their ignorance matched and lodged deep inside them. Here folly is the mind that watches history unfold and completely misses the hand of God's justice in it.
narratives.variation_note: This second reading of the fool (kesil) differs from Psa 49:10 (reading H3684:fool#1), and the difference is a finding. There the fool has one booked act - to perish, alongside the wise and the brutish - a condition levelled by death. Here at Psa 92:6 he is given an active operation ('be a fool') and a target (unable to understand God's ways) - a live blindness to God's justice in history, paired with the stupid man. It differs again from Psa 94:8 (reading #3), where the fool actively believes God does not see and is rebuked. This reading foregrounds the fool's incapacity to read God's justice in the flourishing and doom of the wicked.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fools' (kesil) - the thick-headed, here rebuked. Type (102) is status: a condition of the persons. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fools - the dullest of the people, addressed directly. Operation (106) is 'be foolish': the event is their foolishness in action, the stance behind their claim that the LORD does not see. Target (107) is 'refusing to be wise' (inferred): the folly aims at, or persists in, a refusal - 'when will you be wise?' - the fools holding out against understanding. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with the call to be wise' - so the folly is welded to the summons that they become wise and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the folly is coupled to the call to wisdom and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the senseless who think God does not see, folly rebuked. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the fools are foolish in action - persisting in the notion that the LORD does not see, refusing to be wise - their folly welded to the very call to wisdom that rebukes them and held within. The finding is that this folly is a chosen dullness under direct challenge: 'Fools, when will you be wise?' The One who planted the ear and formed the eye does hear and see, and the fools' senselessness is the refusal to reckon with that - a folly answerable to a summons it keeps resisting.
narratives.story: This psalm rounds on people who tell themselves the Lord does not see and the God of Jacob takes no notice. To them it says, bluntly: understand, you dullest of people - fools, when will you be wise? Their folly is active here: a settled dullness behind the lie that God is not watching. And it is held up against a direct challenge to change - the whole point is the call, when will you be wise? The One who made the ear can obviously hear, and the One who made the eye can obviously see; the fools' senselessness is simply refusing to face that. So their folly is not innocent ignorance but a stubborn refusal, thrown back at them with a summons they keep resisting: stop being foolish and finally come to your senses.
narratives.variation_note: This third reading of the fool (kesil) differs from the other two, and the difference is a finding. At Psa 49:10 (reading #1) the fool is levelled by death; at Psa 92:6 (reading #2) he cannot understand God's justice in history. Here at Psa 94:8 the fool actively believes God does not see and is directly rebuked - his folly coupled to a summons to become wise. This reading foregrounds folly as a chosen, challengeable dullness: not a fate and not merely an incapacity, but a refusal answerable to the direct call 'when will you be wise?'
