narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be wise' (sakal) - to gain discernment. Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent the fools are urged toward, not a single act. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fools - the very dullards of v8, now pressed toward wisdom. Operation (106) is 'become wise': the event is the turn urged on them, from folly toward discernment. Target (107) is 'toward God' (inferred): the wisdom aims Godward - to reckon rightly with the God who hears and sees. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and whether they turn is left open. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with the folly rebuked' - so the wisdom urged is welded to the folly it would replace and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the wisdom is coupled to the rebuked folly and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wisdom the fools are urged toward, the discernment they lack. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the fools are summoned to become wise - a disposition toward God, welded to the very folly it would replace, held as an inner condition. The finding is that wisdom appears here as the demanded alternative to folly: the same verse that rebukes the dull ('when will you be wise?') holds out the discernment they lack, wisdom defined precisely against the senselessness of imagining God does not see. It is the discernment that reckons with the God who made the ear and the eye.
narratives.story: In the same breath that scolds the fools, the psalm holds out the way forward: when will you be wise? Here wisdom is the very thing they are missing - the discernment that would let them see straight. It is offered as the settled alternative to their folly, defined against it: instead of imagining God does not notice, become wise enough to reckon with the God who made the ear and the eye, who obviously hears and sees. The passage does not say whether they will take the turn; it simply names the discernment they lack and presses them toward it. So wisdom shows up here as the demanded cure for folly - the good sense to face God as he really is, pressed on people who have been living as if he were blind.
narratives.variation_note: The same idea of becoming wise appears at Psa 2:10 (reading H7919:wise#1), and the difference is a finding. There rebel kings mid-revolt are summoned to prudence as a cognition - a sharp turn commanded to the powerful. Here at Psa 94:8 the fools are urged toward wisdom as a disposition - a settled discernment they lack, defined against their folly of thinking God does not see. This reading foregrounds wisdom as the standing alternative to dull senselessness before God; the other foregrounds it as an urgent reconsideration demanded of those in active rebellion.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'teach' (chakam, here to make wise) - Joseph teaching Egypt's elders. Type (102) is action: a doing, the imparting of wisdom to others. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind Joseph's teaching. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the teaching is his act, not an inner organ. Bearer (105) is Joseph - the once-imprisoned Hebrew now set over Egypt. Operation (106) is 'teach wisdom': the event is his instructing, wisdom conveyed to the powerful. Target (107) is 'to Pharaoh's elders' (inferred): whom he teaches - Egypt's own counsellors and elders. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with binding princes at his pleasure' - so the teaching is welded to his authority over Egypt's princes and held as an inner condition/capacity. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the teaching is coupled to his rule over the princes and located within as his own wisdom.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): Joseph the wise, instructing Egypt's counsellors, affliction turned to influence. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, Joseph acts to teach wisdom to Pharaoh's elders, the teaching welded to his newly given authority to bind princes and held as his own inner wisdom. The finding is the reversal it caps: the prisoner is now the instructor of a nation's counsellors - affliction turned to influence, the Hebrew slave made the teacher of Egypt's wise. Here wisdom is a gift powerful enough that its bearer, once in chains, ends up schooling the elders of an empire.
narratives.story: This short passage recalls Joseph's astonishing rise. The king who had imprisoned him sets him free and makes him ruler over all his house - and part of what he is given to do is to teach the elders of Egypt wisdom. The once-jailed Hebrew is now the instructor of a great nation's counsellors. His teaching goes hand in hand with his new authority: he can bind Egypt's princes as he pleases and school its elders in wisdom. The wisdom is his own, and it is powerful enough to turn a prisoner into the teacher of an empire's wise men. The whole thing caps a stunning reversal - affliction turned into influence, the slave become the sage who instructs those who once held all the power.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'learn' (lamad) - here learning what is evil. Type (102) is action: a doing, the taking-in of others' ways. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind the learning. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the fathers - Israel's ancestors, who mixed with the nations. Operation (106) is 'learn': the event is their learning, absorbing foreign practice. Target (107) is 'to do as the nations did' (inferred): what they learned - the pagan ways of the surrounding peoples. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked (the idolatry and its curse follow in the psalm but are not booked here). Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with mixing' - so the learning is welded to their mixing with the nations and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the learning is coupled to the mingling and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the adoption of pagan ways, sin caught by association. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, the fathers learn to do as the nations did - a learning welded to their mixing with those nations and held as an inner condition. The finding, read at full weight, is learning in its dark form: the good human capacity to learn here absorbs evil. Sin is caught by association - they mingle with the nations and take on their ways, the very faculty that should acquire wisdom instead soaking up idolatry.
narratives.story: This verse traces how Israel's ancestors went wrong: they mixed with the surrounding nations and learned to do as they did. Learning here is the ordinary human power to pick things up from others - but what they picked up was evil. By mingling with pagan peoples, they absorbed pagan ways, and the mixing and the learning were really one movement. Sin was caught, as it were, by association. It is a sobering picture of how the mind's good ability to learn can work against a person: the very capacity that should be taking in wisdom instead soaked up the practices of idolatry, simply because they kept the wrong company. What you surround yourself with, you learn - and here what they learned undid them.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb (lamad) reads in the opposite direction at Psa 119:7 (reading H3925:learn#2), and the contrast is a finding. Here at Psa 106:35 the learning is a descent: the fathers learn to do as the pagan nations did, evil caught by association, welded to their mixing with the nations. At Psa 119:7 the same verb is an ascent: the psalmist learns God's righteous rules as the ground of upright praise. Same faculty of learning, opposite content - this reading foregrounds learning as the intake of evil through bad company, the other as the intake of God's word.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fools' (eviyl) - the morally foolish, here brought low by their sin. Type (102) is status: a condition of the persons. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the sick - one of the four groups of the redeemed in the psalm, here the afflicted whose trouble came of their folly. Operation (106) is 'be fools': the event is their being foolish, the stance that led into sin. Target (107) is 'through sinful ways' (inferred): the folly runs through their sinful ways - foolishness expressed as the transgression that sickened them. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and the resulting affliction, though named in the passage, is carried by the coupling rather than booked as effect. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with their sinful ways and iniquities' - so the folly is welded to their sinful ways and iniquities and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the folly is coupled to the sinful ways and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the foolish whose sin brought sickness, the third plight. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, these people are fools through their sinful ways - a folly welded to their iniquities and held as an inner condition, issuing in the affliction that brings them to death's gates until they cry to the LORD. The finding is folly's bodily cost: this is not folly in the abstract but foolishness lived out as sin, which loathes food and draws near to death - senselessness that literally makes a person ill until God's word heals him.
narratives.story: This part of the psalm tells of people who suffered because of their own foolishness: some were fools through their sinful ways, and their iniquities brought them to misery. Their folly was not a harmless quirk; it worked itself out as sin, and the sin made them ill - so sick they could not stand the sight of food and came right up to the gates of death. The foolishness and the sinful ways were bound together, lodged deep inside them. Only when they cried out to the Lord in their trouble did he send his word and heal them. Here folly is shown at real bodily cost: living senselessly, against God, is not just a mistake in the mind but something that can break a person's body and bring them to the edge of the grave.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wits' (chokmah) - here practical skill, the sailors' seamanship. Type (102) is faculty: a capacity, the competence one relies on. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the sailors - the seafarers caught in God's storm. Operation (106) is 'be at their wits' end': the event is the collapse of their skill, competence exhausted. Target (107) is 'in the storm' (inferred): the setting and object of the failure - the raging sea that undoes them. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with reeling and staggering' - so the failure of wits is welded to their reeling and staggering like drunk men and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the exhausted skill is coupled to their staggering and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the sailors' skill exhausted, seamanship undone by the sea. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the sailors' practical wisdom collapses - they are at their wits' end in the storm, their skill welded to the reeling and staggering that mark its failure, held as an inner condition. The finding is wisdom's exhaustion: this chokmah is not moral or godly insight but competence, and the point is that it runs out. Faced with a sea God raises, the most skilled seamen are undone - all their wits swallowed up - until they cry to the LORD and he stills the storm. Here even good, real skill has a limit, and the limit is God's power in the deep.
narratives.story: This part of the psalm describes sailors caught in a storm that God himself raised. The waves fling their ship up to the sky and down to the depths, and the experienced seamen are at their wits' end. Their 'wits' here are their skill, their hard-won seamanship - and it simply runs out. They reel and stagger about the deck like drunk men, all their competence useless against the sea. There is no lack of ability in them; it is just that their ability has a limit, and the storm is past it. Only when they cry out to the Lord does he hush the wind and calm the waves. Here the passage shows that even genuine, practical skill can be completely overwhelmed - and when it is, the sailors have nowhere to turn but to the God who holds the sea.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wise' (chakam) - the discerning person at the psalm's close. Type (102) is status: a settled condition of insight. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is whoever is wise - the open invitation of the coda, any who will attend. Operation (106) is 'be wise': the event is the exercise of wisdom, attending and considering. Target (107) is 'to attend to God's ways' (inferred): what the wisdom does - fasten on these things, consider the steadfast love of the LORD. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with attending and considering' - so the wisdom is welded to the acts of attending and considering and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the wisdom is coupled to attending/considering and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wise who read God's dealings, the coda's charge. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, whoever is wise attends to these things - wisdom exercised as the reading of God's dealings, welded to the acts of attending and considering the steadfast love of the LORD, held as an inner condition. The finding is what wisdom is for: after the long psalm of the LORD's rescues, wisdom is defined as the capacity to look back over such dealings and see God's steadfast love in them. To be wise is to attend and consider - to read the LORD's providence rightly. Wisdom here is not cleverness but the discerning heart that draws the lesson from what God has done.
narratives.story: The long psalm has told story after story of people in trouble crying out and the Lord rescuing them. At the end it turns to the reader and says: whoever is wise, let him attend to these things and consider the steadfast love of the Lord. Here wisdom is exactly this - the ability to look back over all that God has done and actually see his faithful love running through it. The wise person is not the cleverest but the one who pays attention and reflects, who reads God's dealings rightly and takes the lesson to heart. The invitation is open to anyone willing to do it. So wisdom is given a job: to consider God's works of rescue and draw from them the truth about his steadfast love. To be wise is to notice, and to understand what you are seeing.
narratives.variation_note: The same word (chakam) reads very differently at Psa 49:10 (reading H2450:wise#1), and the contrast is a finding. There the wise man is caught under mortality - his one booked act is to die, levelled with the fool and the brutish, wisdom shown at its limit. Here at Psa 107:43 the wise man is at the height of his powers: attending to God's dealings and discerning the steadfast love of the LORD in them. This reading foregrounds wisdom as the discerning reading of God's providence; the other foregrounds wisdom overtaken by death.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'wisdom' (chokmah) - here the wisdom that begins in the fear of God. Type (102) is disposition: a settled bent, grown from a root, not a possessed store nor a single act. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though the operation names its root - the fear of the LORD. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the God-fearing - those who fear the LORD, in whom wisdom takes its start. Operation (106) is 'gain wisdom': the event is the acquiring of wisdom, its beginning. Target (107) is 'from fearing God' (inferred): the wisdom is drawn from the fear of the LORD - reverence is the source-within-the-event. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with the fear of the LORD' - so the wisdom is welded to the fear of the LORD and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the wisdom is coupled to the fear of the LORD and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wisdom that flows from the fear of God, its root and source. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no separately booked source but with the fear of the LORD named as its root, the God-fearing gain wisdom - a disposition welded to that reverence and held as an inner condition. The finding is the root: this wisdom does not begin in intelligence or study but in the fear of the LORD; reverence is where understanding starts, and those who practise it have good understanding. Wisdom here is grown from awe of God - the first move of a mind rightly ordered toward him.
narratives.story: This psalm of praise ends with a famous line: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Here wisdom is traced to its root, and the root is reverence - a right awe of God. Real wisdom does not start with cleverness or education; it starts with fearing the Lord, and it grows in those who live that way. The passage adds that all who practise it have good understanding. So wisdom is pictured as a settled bent of the inner life that takes its very first breath from the fear of God. Bound up with reverence, it is the mind rightly ordered toward the Lord. To become wise, on this account, you begin not by getting smarter but by standing in awe of God - and everything else follows from there.
narratives.variation_note: This fourth wisdom (chokmah) reading, like Psa 90:12, traces wisdom to a root rather than describing its exercise - but the roots differ, and that is the finding. At Psa 90:12 wisdom is gained by numbering our days, the fruit of facing death; here at Psa 111:10 it flows from the fear of the LORD. Both differ from Psa 49:3 (a teacher's possessed store) and Psa 51:6 (wisdom implanted by God in the secret heart). This reading foregrounds reverence as the very beginning of wisdom - the first ordering of the mind toward God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'simple' (pethi) - the artless, childlike, easily-swayed. Type (102) is status: a condition of the person, here owned by the psalmist. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the simple - the naive whom the LORD keeps, among whom the psalmist counts himself. Operation (106) is 'be preserved': the event booked is not the simple person doing anything but his being kept - the LORD preserves the simple. Target (107) is 'by God' (inferred): the agent of the preserving - it is God who guards them. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked beyond the preserving itself. Coupling (112) and locus (116) together bind the reading: the two rows carry an internal:ib-state marker and 'paired with being brought low and saved' - so the simplicity is welded to the psalmist's being brought low and saved and held as an inner condition. (The rows appear transposed against their labels; read for content, the simplicity is coupled to his being brought low and saved, and located within.) Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the artless, the childlike, whom God keeps; the psalmist owns himself among them. Role (115) is characteristic. The full process: with no source and no seat, the simple are preserved by God - the one movement is not their act but God's keeping of them, welded to the psalmist's own being brought low and then saved, held as an inner condition. The finding is unexpectedly tender: within a family full of folly condemned, 'simple' is read not as culpable but as the childlike lowliness God protects. The psalmist, brought low, does not claim to be shrewd; he owns himself among the simple - and finds that the very ones without cleverness are the ones the LORD preserves.
narratives.story: In a psalm of thanksgiving for rescue from death, the psalmist says something humble and warm: the Lord preserves the simple. The 'simple' are the artless, childlike people who are easily swayed and have no great cleverness to protect themselves. Here they are not blamed for it - they are kept safe by God. And the psalmist puts himself among them: when I was brought low, he saved me. He does not claim to have been shrewd or self-sufficient; he admits he was one of the simple, brought low, and it was the Lord who guarded and rescued him. In a study full of folly being condemned, this is a gentler note: sometimes being simple means being lowly and defenceless in a way that God does not despise but protects. The ones without cleverness are exactly the ones he keeps.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'learn' (lamad) - here learning God's righteous rules. Type (102) is action: a doing, the taking-in of God's word. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - the lover of the law who wants to learn it. Operation (106) is 'learn': the event is his learning, the intake of God's rules. Target (107) is 'God's word' (inferred): what he learns - the righteous rules, the law of the LORD. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, and the fruit (upright praise) is carried by the passage rather than booked as effect. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): the learning is welded to its recurrence through Psalm 119, part of a sustained arc of learning God's word (see the recurrences below). Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): learning the rules as the ground of upright praise - 'I will praise you with an upright heart, when I learn your righteous rules.' Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is external:god - the learning is oriented outside the self, toward God and his word; its reference-point is the LORD. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, the psalmist learns God's righteous rules - an action oriented toward God (external:god), welded across the psalm into a sustained arc of learning, and set as the very ground of upright praise. The finding is the direction: unlike the fathers of Psalm 106 who learned evil, here learning is the intake of God's word, and it is the condition of true worship - one can praise with an upright heart only as one learns the rules that make the heart upright. This same learning recurs later in the psalm (vv71, 73), where affliction itself becomes the teacher.
narratives.story: This great psalm on God's law opens with a person who wants to learn it: I will praise you with an upright heart, when I learn your righteous rules. Learning here is the good intake of God's word - taking his commands into oneself. And it is aimed outward, at God: it is his rules the psalmist is bent on learning. Notice how learning and worship are tied together - he can only praise God with a truly upright heart as he learns the rules that set his heart straight. So learning is not just filling the mind with information; it is what makes right praise possible. This same hunger to learn runs on through the psalm - later the writer even says it was good for him to be afflicted, because his suffering taught him God's statutes. Here learning is the lifeline of a heart that wants to belong wholly to God.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb (lamad) reads in the opposite direction at Psa 106:35 (reading H3925:learn#1), and the contrast is a finding. There the fathers learn to do as the pagan nations did - evil caught by association, oriented into the world. Here at Psa 119:7 the psalmist learns God's righteous rules - oriented toward God (external:god) and set as the ground of upright praise. Same faculty of learning, opposite content and direction: this reading foregrounds learning as the intake of God's word that makes worship possible, the other as the intake of evil through bad company.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be wise' (chakam) - here 'wiser', made more discerning than one's enemies. Type (102) is disposition: a settled condition of insight, received and held. Source (103) is absent as a booked row, though the verse names the giver - God's commandment. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - who finds himself outstripping his enemies in wisdom. Operation (106) is 'be made wiser': the event is his being rendered wiser - a passive making, the commandment working the wisdom. Target (107) is none: no object the wisdom is aimed at is booked - the reading reports the wisdom conferred, not pointed at a further end. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' (inferred): the wisdom is welded to its recurrence through Psalm 119, part of the sustained arc of the word forming the psalmist's understanding. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): the wisdom the ever-present commandment gives - 'Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me.' Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no separately booked source but with God's commandment named as the giver, the psalmist is made wiser than his enemies - a disposition received, welded across the psalm into the arc of the word forming him, and held as an inner condition. The finding is the ground of the wisdom: it is not native talent but the commandment 'ever with me' - constant companionship with God's word that outfits the psalmist beyond his enemies, his teachers, and the aged (vv98-100). Wisdom here is the yield of the word kept always near.
narratives.story: In the long psalm on God's law, the writer makes a bold claim: your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me. His wisdom is not something he was born with or figured out on his own; it is worked into him by God's command, which he keeps constantly at his side. Because the word is always with him, he ends up wiser than his enemies, wiser even than his teachers and the aged - not through cleverness but through steady companionship with what God has said. The wisdom is a settled quality of his inner life, and it is entirely the fruit of keeping God's word close. The lesson is quiet but strong: real understanding comes not from raw brilliance but from living, day and night, with the word of God near at hand.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'desire to be taught God's will' - a longing for instruction, read off 'teach me to do your will.' Type (102) is volition: an act of the will, the interior wanting to be shaped. Source (103) is absent: no origin is booked behind the longing. Seat (104) is none: not organ-located; the desire is the whole self's, not an organ's. Bearer (105) is the psalmist - hunted, fainting in spirit, turning to God. Operation (106) is the core event: the self asks to be taught to do God's will, wanting the good Spirit to lead it on level ground. Target (107) is 'teachability' (inferred): what the operation aims at is a taught, conformed interior - not mere rescue but obedience learned. Manner (108) is none. Intensity (109), specifier (110), and effect (111) are absent: no degree is scored, nothing narrows it, no outcome booked. Coupling (112) is 'teach-me-your-will' (inferred): the volition is welded to its very content, the plea to be taught God's will. Prohibition (113) is absent. Discovery (114): beyond guidance-for-safety - the interior wants conformity, to be led on level ground; not just direction but a taught will. Role (115) is characteristic. Locus (116) is internal:ib-state - a condition of the inner life. The full process: with no booked source and no seat, the psalmist's will reaches out and asks to be taught to do God's will, wanting the good Spirit to lead it level - a volition welded to that plea, aimed at a teachable, conformed interior, held within. The finding is the depth of the request: pressed hard by enemies, he asks not merely to be shown a safe path but to be taught obedience itself - the inner life wanting to be conformed to God's will, not just guided around danger. Here teaching is longed for from the receiving side, the hunger of a heart that wants to be made obedient.
narratives.story: Hunted and worn down, his spirit failing, the psalmist prays for something deeper than escape: teach me to do your will, for you are my God. He is not just asking for directions out of trouble; he is asking to be taught obedience itself, to have his will shaped so that he actually does what God wants, led on level ground by God's good Spirit. This is an act of longing - a heart reaching out to be instructed and conformed. What he wants is a teachable, obedient inner life, not merely a safe way through his enemies. It is striking that, in the middle of real danger, his deepest request is to be made the kind of person who does God's will. Here the hunger to be taught comes from the inside, from someone who wants God not only to rescue him but to remake how he lives.
narratives.variation_note: The same verb for teaching (lamad) appears at Psa 34:11 (reading H3925:teach#1), and the direction reverses - the finding. There the psalmist is the teacher, willing to hand the fear of the LORD to children (outward, giving). Here at Psa 143:10 he is the pupil, asking God to teach him to do his will (inward, receiving) - not guidance for safety but conformity of the will, the hunger to be made obedient. Both are acts of the will about instruction, but this reading foregrounds the longing to be taught oneself, while the other foregrounds the desire to teach others.
